claims.text: The baseline material is FeCoNiCrAl feedstock with a particle-size distribution of 15–45 μm deposited by APS.
A localized argon or high-purity-nitrogen shroud can envelope the APS spray plume.
The localized shroud will maintain an inert atmosphere around the particle stream during otherwise standard ambient APS deposition.
Inert-gas shrouding will reduce contact between molten particles and atmospheric oxygen during flight.
Reduced oxygen contact will decrease premature in-flight oxidation of FeCoNiCrAl particles.
Reducing oxide formation on molten particle surfaces will improve splat formation and inter-splat bonding.
Preserving a more uniform molten-particle state will improve splat coalescence upon impact.
Fully molten particles with sufficient velocity form well-flattened splats, whereas insufficiently molten particles may rebound or remain as unmelted inclusions.
Improved splat coalescence and inter-splat bonding will produce a denser coating.
Inert-gas shrouding will improve deposition efficiency.
Improved deposition efficiency will produce a thicker FeCoNiCrAl coating than unshrouded APS using the same 15–45 μm feedstock.
The shrouded coating will be denser than the unshrouded baseline coating.
The shrouded coating will exhibit minimal as-sprayed oxidation relative to the baseline.
The resulting coating will maintain mechanical integrity suitable for high-temperature service as a thermal-barrier-system bond coat.
The unshrouded APS baseline has higher in-flight oxidation than the proposed shrouded process.
The intervention may lose effectiveness if the inert-gas envelope is nonuniform or if the shroud alters spray dynamics.
SEM cross-sections can assess coating thickness and microstructural integrity.
EDS elemental mapping can determine coating oxide content and its distribution.
Failure to obtain both a statistically significant thickness increase and reduced oxidation, or observation of degraded coating integrity, will falsify the hypothesis.
